newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Kabila visits Angola for security talks--diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Kabila visits Angola for security talks--diplomats.

text.p: Congolese President Laurent Kabila flew into Luanda on Tuesday for two days of talks with Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos, which foreign diplomats said would encompass crucial cross-border security issues.

The rebel leader turned president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire, made no comments after his arrival at a Luanda airport where he was greeted by dos Santos and others before being whisked off to the presidential compound.
Congolese Trade and Industry Minister Pierre Victor Mpoyd told reporters Kabila was in Angola "to expand relations between the two countries", without elaborating.

But diplomats and officials in Luanda said Kabila was expected to play a vital role in how the Angolan government deals with the former UNITA rebels -- once strongly allied to ousted Zairean leader Mobutu Sese Seko -- who still control most of the Angolan countryside.
Kabila has emerged as one of Angola's key allies in the region since his rise to power in May after ousting Mobutu. The Angolan government was long suspected of supporting Kabila against Mobutu.
Now diplomats and officials close to the drawn-out Angolan peace process believe Kabila is ready to support the Angolan government if it decides to try to defeat UNITA militarily.
"They (Kabila and dos Santos) will talk about a number of things. But they are also going to talk about UNITA," one diplomat said.

"Obviously when and if war breaks out, they want to make sure all the arrangements are in place for forces from both countries to cross the border. If the FAA (Angolan army) wants to do hot pursuit of UNITA into Congo there has to be a mechanism," the diplomat said.

The former rebels from UNITA (the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) are under threat by the United Nations Security Council to reply to a series of demands by August 15 or face stiff new sanctions.
The Security Council has demanded that UNITA define the number of troops it still has under arms and renew a programme of turning over its territory to the government.

UNITA's perceived intransigence on the demands, and the government's military build-up, have brought the country's peace process -- now almost three years old -- to the brink of collapse, diplomats said.

"I think it's obvious what's going on here," one Western diplomat told Reuters. "Dos Santos is making sure that he works things out with Kabila before they launch any kind of offensive against UNITA. They will cover other issues too, but the main topic here is UNITA."
On Monday the U.N. Observer Mission and the three observer missions to the peace process, America, Russia and Portugal, called a recent UNITA proposal for handing over its territory "unacceptable".

A press release made available on Tuesday said "Taking into account the gravity of the situation (we) urge UNITA to act transparently and with speed so that it provides the information demanded by the Security Council..."
One official close to the peace process, which ended two decades of civil war, told Reuters: "I have never been more concerned about the peace process -- or of the threat of war -- than I am now."
